excerpt: When a visitor walked into the Island Locator office carrying a small box of World War II Kodachrome slides, the past stopped being a matter of black-and-white photographs. Here is the story of Sergeant Raymond Hagley, the rare color images he made on Saipan, and the family who brought them back home.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
When you work for a small island magazine, history rarely arrives in a grand procession. More often, it walks through the front door carrying a small box and a quiet set of memories.

That was how I met Greg Hagley and his two sons. They had traveled a long way to these islands, bringing a rare cargo: a handful of Kodachrome slides taken during the Second World War by Greg’s father, Staff Sergeant Raymond Hagley.

In those days, war was recorded mostly in shades of charcoal and gray. But Ray Hagley was an artist—a young man who had toured with swing bands and crossed paths with Glenn Miller before the draft found him in 1943. When the Army Air Force sent him to Saipan with the 73rd Bombardment Wing, he brought along a Kine Exakta 35mm camera and a few rolls of color film.

Listening to the family talk, you could sense how much those small squares of celluloid meant to them. Greg recalled his father telling stories of the long flight across the Pacific in a windowless plane, and of the heat on Saipan, where airmen washed away the salt and dust off Ladder Beach. Between missions, Ray painted nose art on the bombers and looked at the island through his lens. While others saw only scorched ground and military routine, Ray saw color: the deep blue of the Pacific, the green of the palms, the bright red of sunlit soil.

Ray died in 1991, leaving the slides tucked away in Cleveland. Years later, his family uncovered them—a dozen bright moments saved from a summer long ago. In 2007, Greg and his sons made the trip to Saipan to present the images to the local government, and they were generous enough to let our magazine share them.

Holding those slides up to the light, decades after the shutter clicked, felt like looking through a clean window into a distant afternoon. War has a way of turning men into numbers and places into maps. But in Ray’s Kodachrome hues, the sky is blue again, the men are young, and the island stands still.
title: Ray Hagley's Saipan in Color
